title: Matrix Product State Theory of Few-Photon Squeezed Pulses Interacting with a Two-Level Emitter in a Waveguide
authors: Sofia Arranz Regidor, Matthew Kozma, Stephen Hughes
abstract: Squeezed light states have a special place in quantum optics with potentially profound applications in emerging quantum technologies. We present a numerically-exact matrix product states (MPS) approach to model quantum pulses of squeezed light, at the few-photon level, interacting with a two-level system in a waveguide environment. We represent the squeezed state as a coherent superposition of Fock states and explore the nonlinear population dynamics as well as multi-photon correlation functions that emerge. We show how the squeezed pulse can create quantum correlations that are unique to squeezed pulses, including $\langle b(t) b(t+t')\rangle$ for transmitted fields as well as $\langle b^\dagger(t) b^\dagger(t+t') b(t+t') b(t) \rangle$. We also demonstrate how $\langle b(t) b(t+t') \rangle$, a first-order correlation function, shows nonlinear photon correlations that are similar to those known and measured for two-photon scattering states. Finally, we also study the squeezed spectra of the pulse before and after interacting with the two-level system, and highlight the role of the spectral bandwidth of the incident pulse. The MPS theory allows the modeling of arbitrary bandwidth squeezing without making any Markov and Born approximations for the light-matter interaction processes, and can easily be extended to waveguide systems with multiple emitters and time-delayed feedback.
summary: The authors present a numerically exact Matrix Product States (MPS) method to simulate how few-photon squeezed light interacts with a two-level emitter in a waveguide. This approach allows for modeling non-Markovian dynamics without standard approximations. Key findings demonstrate that the interaction significantly reshapes and alters the spectral properties of the transmitted squeezed pulse, providing detailed insight into quantum correlation generation.
main_problem: The study focuses on modeling the quantum dynamics of few-photon squeezed light pulses as they interact with a two-level emitter (TLS) embedded in a waveguide environment.
main_result: The MPS approach successfully models non-Markovian interactions, showing that the TLS interaction causes unique nonlinear reshaping and sign flips in the transmitted squeezing spectrum compared to the input pulse.
method: A numerically exact Matrix Product States (MPS) formalism is employed to simulate the time evolution of the quantum state, avoiding standard Markov or Born approximations.
model_or_system: The system consists of a squeezed light field propagating in a waveguide and coupled to a TLS. The Hamiltonian includes terms for the waveguide modes, the TLS, and their interaction, which is discretized into time-bin noise operators for simulation.
key_observables: Multi-photon correlation functions (e.g., $\langle b(t)b(t + t')angle$), nonlinear population dynamics ($n_{TLS}$), transmitted photon flux ($n_R$), and the squeezed spectrum $S(\omega, \phi)$.
important_parameters: The squeezing parameter ($\zeta$), pulse temporal length (bandwidth), and the coupling strength of the TLS are key parameters varied in the analysis.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the MPS framework can accurately capture the dynamics across arbitrary bandwidths without resorting to Markovian approximations, though initial focus may be on weak regimes dominated by 2-photon subspaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of input vs. transmitted squeezing spectra for varying pulse lengths, and compare TLS population dynamics and output flux using MPS results against master equation benchmarks.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model (squeezed light + TLS in a waveguide), develops the MPS methodology to handle non-Markovian time evolution, calculates key correlation functions and spectral responses, and compares these findings against established approximations.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of open quantum system simulation by applying MPS theory to model complex, non-Markovian light-matter interactions in waveguide QED, which is a core area of AMO physics.

We see a bird-like feature emerging that is similar to the 2-photon Fock state solution for second-order correlation functions [60– 62].
